title: Drug Information and Pharmacovigilance
description: Drug information services, literature evaluation, adverse drug reactions and their reporting, medication errors, and drug safety systems in Nigeria.

topics.title: Drug Information Services
topics.summary: Sources of information, answering drug queries systematically, and evaluating literature.

notes.b: Drug information sources are tertiary (textbooks, compendia and databases — e.g. British National Formulary (BNF), BNF for Children, Martindale, the Nigerian National Drug Formulary and Essential Medicines List, product information leaflets/SmPCs, WHO Model Formulary; quick but may be outdated), secondary (indexing and abstracting services — PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library) and primary (original research — clinical trials, cohort studies, case reports). A systematic approach to a drug information query: identify the requester and their background, obtain complete background information (patient details, the real question), categorise the query, develop a search strategy (tertiary → secondary → primary), evaluate and synthesise the evidence, formulate and communicate a response (timely, clear, referenced), and document and follow up.
k: Get background — find the real question

notes.b: Critical appraisal assesses validity, results and applicability. The hierarchy of evidence places systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs at the top, followed by RCTs, cohort studies, case–control studies, case series/reports and expert opinion. Key RCT questions: was randomisation adequate and concealed? Were groups similar at baseline? Was blinding used? Was analysis by intention to treat? Was follow-up complete? Results are expressed as relative risk, absolute risk reduction (ARR), relative risk reduction (RRR), number needed to treat (NNT = 1/ARR), odds ratios, hazard ratios and confidence intervals (a 95% CI of a ratio that crosses 1 means no significant difference). Beware industry-funded promotional material and surrogate outcomes; distinguish statistical from clinical significance.

topics.title: Adverse Drug Reactions
topics.summary: Definitions, classification (Rawlins–Thompson), risk factors and causality assessment.

notes.b: An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a response to a medicine that is noxious and unintended, occurring at doses normally used in humans. An adverse event is any untoward occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug. Side effects are unintended effects related to pharmacological properties (may be beneficial or harmful). The Rawlins–Thompson classification (extended): Type A (augmented — dose-related, predictable, common, from known pharmacology, e.g. bleeding with warfarin, hypoglycaemia with sulfonylureas), Type B (bizarre — not dose-related, unpredictable, often immunological or idiosyncratic, e.g. anaphylaxis to penicillin, Stevens–Johnson syndrome with sulfonamides or nevirapine), Type C (chronic — e.g. adrenal suppression with steroids), Type D (delayed — e.g. teratogenesis, carcinogenesis), Type E (end-of-use — withdrawal, e.g. rebound hypertension after clonidine) and Type F (failure of therapy — e.g. interactions reducing contraceptive efficacy). A serious ADR results in death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs hospitalisation, causes disability, or a congenital anomaly.
k: C chronic, D delayed, E end-of-use, F failure

notes.b: Risk factors: extremes of age, female sex, polypharmacy, renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, genetic factors (e.g. G6PD deficiency — haemolysis with primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides; common in Nigeria; HLA-B*5701 and abacavir), previous ADRs, and HIV infection (higher rates of cutaneous reactions to cotrimoxazole). Causality assessment uses the WHO-UMC system (certain, probable/likely, possible, unlikely, conditional, unassessable) or the Naranjo algorithm (a scored questionnaire: definite ≥ 9, probable 5–8, possible 1–4, doubtful ≤ 0). Key considerations: temporal relationship, dechallenge (improvement on withdrawal), rechallenge (recurrence on re-exposure — rarely done deliberately), alternative causes and previous reports.

topics.title: Pharmacovigilance Systems
topics.summary: Spontaneous reporting, NAFDAC's National Pharmacovigilance Centre, signal detection and post-marketing surveillance.

notes.b: Pharmacovigilance is the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding and prevention of adverse effects or any other medicine-related problem (WHO). Clinical trials are too small and short to detect rare or delayed ADRs, so post-marketing surveillance is essential (e.g. thalidomide disaster). Spontaneous (passive) reporting is the backbone: in Nigeria, health workers and patients report suspected ADRs to NAFDAC's National Pharmacovigilance Centre (NPC, established 2004; a full member of the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring) using the yellow ADR reporting form, the Med Safety app or e-reporting. Reports should be made even if causality is uncertain. Limitations: under-reporting (the major problem), reporting bias and no denominator. Reports enter the WHO global database VigiBase (managed by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre, Sweden).
k: Trials too small for rare ADRs
Yellow form and Med Safety app

notes.b: Active surveillance methods include cohort event monitoring (following all patients receiving a new medicine — used in Nigeria for ACTs and antiretrovirals), sentinel sites, targeted spontaneous reporting (e.g. TB and HIV programmes), registries (e.g. pregnancy exposure registries) and record linkage. A signal is reported information on a possible causal relationship between an adverse event and a drug, previously unknown or incompletely documented; signals are detected by clinical review and disproportionality analysis (e.g. reporting odds ratio, information component), then evaluated. Regulatory actions include label changes, 'Dear Healthcare Professional' letters, restricted use, and withdrawal. Public health programmes (malaria, HIV, TB, immunisation — AEFI surveillance) integrate pharmacovigilance. Poor-quality and falsified medicines are also monitored.
k: Regulatory actions: label change to withdrawal

topics.title: Medication Errors and Patient Safety
topics.summary: Types and causes of medication errors, prevention strategies and reporting culture.

notes.b: A medication error is any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the health professional, patient or consumer. Errors occur at prescribing (wrong drug, dose, illegible handwriting, ambiguous abbreviations such as 'U' for units or 'qd'), transcribing, dispensing (look-alike sound-alike drugs, wrong strength), administration (wrong route, time, patient; IV rate errors) and monitoring stages. Contributing factors: workload, fatigue, poor communication, knowledge gaps, poor labelling and packaging, and lack of systems. Reason's 'Swiss cheese' model explains how multiple system failures align to cause harm. Preventable ADRs overlap with medication errors. The WHO Global Patient Safety Challenge 'Medication Without Harm' aimed to reduce severe avoidable medication-related harm by 50%.

Prevention strategies: the 'rights' of medication administration (right patient, drug, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response), computerised prescribing with decision support, barcode administration, standardised concentrations, independent double checks for high-alert medicines, tall-man lettering, separating LASA products, clear labelling, avoiding error-prone abbreviations, pharmacist review of prescriptions, medication reconciliation at transitions of care, and patient education (patients as partners). A just, non-punitive culture encourages reporting and learning; root cause analysis investigates serious incidents, and near misses are valuable learning opportunities. Paediatric dosing errors (tenfold errors from misplaced decimal points — never use trailing zeros, e.g. write 1 mg not 1.0 mg; always use a leading zero, 0.5 mg not .5 mg) are especially dangerous.
k: No trailing zeros; always leading zero

topics.title: Drug Interactions and Special Populations
topics.summary: Mechanisms of interactions, clinically important examples, and prescribing in pregnancy, children, elderly and organ impairment.

notes.b: Pharmacokinetic interactions alter absorption (e.g. tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones chelated by antacids, iron, calcium), distribution (protein binding displacement — usually minor), metabolism (enzyme inducers — rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, efavirenz, St John's wort — reduce levels of oral contraceptives, warfarin and antiretrovirals; inhibitors — ketoconazole, erythromycin/clarithromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice, cimetidine — increase levels, e.g. simvastatin toxicity) and excretion (probenecid reduces penicillin excretion; NSAIDs and diuretics raise lithium levels). Pharmacodynamic interactions are additive, synergistic or antagonistic (e.g. QT-prolonging drugs combined, serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and tramadol, NSAIDs with anticoagulants increasing bleeding). Rifampicin with antiretrovirals and hormonal contraceptives is a major concern in TB/HIV care in Nigeria.

Pregnancy: avoid known teratogens (ACE inhibitors, warfarin, isotretinoin, valproate, methotrexate, tetracyclines); use drugs with established safety (e.g. methyldopa, nifedipine and labetalol for hypertension; folic acid). Breastfeeding: most drugs are compatible; consider infant exposure. Children: doses by weight or body surface area; immature hepatic and renal function in neonates (chloramphenicol grey baby syndrome); avoid aspirin (Reye's syndrome) and tetracyclines (tooth staining). Elderly: reduced renal function and altered body composition, polypharmacy and falls — use tools like the Beers criteria and STOPP/START; start low, go slow. Renal impairment: adjust doses of renally excreted drugs (aminoglycosides, metformin, digoxin) using creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault). Hepatic impairment: caution with drugs extensively metabolised by the liver and those causing hepatotoxicity.
